description: A vaccine doesn't inject the disease to scare you. It trains your immune system with a harmless version, so it reacts quickly next time.

hero.hook: The vaccine teaches your body to recognize danger... without causing it to experience the real disease.

blocks.text: Vaccines have saved more lives than almost any other medical invention. Smallpox****, which still killed hundreds of millions of people in the 20th century, was eradicated thanks to vaccination.
The principle is simple: show the body a “training mannequin”, so that it creates an **immune memory** without going through the real disease.
When a microbe (virus or bacteria) enters for the first time, it often takes your body **7 to 14 days** to mount an effective defense. During this time, you may be sick.

Certain cells, , produce **antibodies** (proteins that stick to the intruder). Others, , destroy cells already infected. Once the threat has been defeated, part of these cells remain dormant: they are **memory cells**. [[B lymphocytes and antibodies]] [[T lymphocytes]]
If the same microbe comes back, the response goes away much more quickly. Often you don't even get sick. The vaccine creates this memory… without the risk of real infection.

sections.title: The memory of the immune system

blocks.text: **AttenuatedZ**vaccines contain a live microbe, but made very weak (e.g. measles). They train well, but are not recommended if the immune system is very fragile.
**inactivated vaccines** use a killed microbe (e.g. certain flus). More secure, they often require callbacks. **subunit vaccines** only show a piece of the microbe, for example a surface protein.
**Z**mRNA vaccines provide a short instruction: your cells temporarily make a harmless virus protein. Your immunity learns to recognize it. The mRNA then degrades; it does not modify your DNA.
Long before Jenner, a form of “variolization” was already being practiced in China: voluntarily exposing oneself to an attenuated form of smallpox to protect oneself.

sections.title: Several ways to train the body

blocks.text: When enough people are protected, the microbe circulates less. It's the . It also protects those who cannot be vaccinated (newborns, immunocompromised people). [[Group immunity]]
The threshold depends on contagiousness. For **measles**, you often need **92 to 95%** coverage. For polio, rather around **80 to 85%**.
Smallpox was declared eradicated in **1980**. The last known natural case dates from **1977**, in Somalia.
A vaccine goes through strict trials before authorization. Some contain : substances that help the immune system to better “notice” the vaccine. [[Adjuvants]]
Paradoxically, when diseases disappear from daily life, we forget their danger. Measles outbreaks remind us that collective protection remains fragile if coverage declines.
A vaccine trains the immune system with a harmless version of danger. It creates cellular memory, protects the individual, and, on a population scale, slows down or stops epidemics.
